justification: All CHRNA1-specific evidence in this corpus concerns the muscle-type nicotinic acetylcholine receptor alpha1 subunit at the neuromuscular junction: congenital myasthenic syndromes, fetal akinesia/multiple pterygium syndrome, myasthenia gravis susceptibility, and euploid pregnancy loss (PMIDs 27748205, 29478601, 29054425, 19261599, 35074870, 27501803, 31150545). The only epilepsy-focused article (PMID 36796465) implicates neuronal subunits CHRNA4, CHRNB2 and CHRNA2 in sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy and does not attribute any epilepsy role to CHRNA1. Thus CHRNA1 is only co-mentioned with epilepsy through the broader nAChR gene family, which provides a weak, indirect biological rationale at best and no patient-level genetic evidence. A small share of probability is allocated to Hypothesized because of the shared receptor family/cholinergic excitability biology, but no human or animal data link CHRNA1 variants to seizures.

justification: Multiple independent human studies report de novo KCNC1 variants in epilepsy probands with supporting functional data: the recurrent p.Arg320His variant defining MEAK (progressive myoclonus epilepsy with ataxia) was identified in heterozygous patients (PMID 27629860) and characterized in a cohort of 20 cases (PMID 28380698). Independent cohorts expanded the phenotype to developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with recurrent de novo p.Ala421Val in six unrelated patients (PMID 31353855) and five unrelated individuals with three new de novo missense variants (PMID 31353862). Additional de novo variants with epilepsy phenotypes are reported in separate probands (PMIDs 34733949, 37203213, 34232791), and diagnostic cohorts of infantile-onset epilepsy and PME repeatedly identify KCNC1 as causative (PMIDs 33349918, 31216804). Functional electrophysiology (loss- or gain-of-function) supports causality, but the evidence base is primarily human genetic and replicated across independent probands, justifying "Established."

justification: Every article in this set concerns MYH2 as the fast type IIa myosin heavy chain gene causing congenital/hereditary myosin myopathy (ophthalmoplegia, proximal weakness, rimmed vacuoles, loss of type 2A fibers), with no study examining autism spectrum disorder. There is no report of ASD probands, ASD cohorts, or any neurodevelopmental genetic association with MYH2; the gene's known biology is sarcomeric skeletal muscle contraction, not neurodevelopment. The only tangential neurodevelopmental mention is a single case report of a child with motor developmental disorder and intellectual disability carrying MYH2 variants (PMID 30662633), which concerns ID/motor delay rather than ASD and is a single anecdotal case. Another paper (PMID 30009132) lists MYH2 only among neuromuscular findings in a mitochondrial-disease exome cohort, which is incidental. Therefore the evidence base supports "Novel," with a small allowance for a weak "Existing/Hypothesized" reading from the single ID-associated case report.

justification: Three independent primary clinical reports provide variant-level human evidence: PMID 31794024 identified a homozygous non-canonical splice variant (c.454+3A>G) in seven affected children from three unrelated families with early-onset seizures, developmental delay and brain atrophy, with functional validation of aberrant splicing and TRAPP complex destabilization; PMID 32901138 independently reported 23 patients from 17 unrelated families with the same homozygous variant and early-onset epilepsy, confirming pathogenicity via RNA-seq; PMID 34878169 described three individuals from two additional Indian families with novel bi-allelic missense variants and the same epileptic phenotype. These are single-gene point variants (not multigene CNVs) in independent probands, meeting the replication requirement. Supporting mechanistic work in yeast and patient fibroblasts (PMID 32116085) reinforces causality, and other reports (PMID 32125366, 32125358) corroborate the recurrent variant. The remaining TRAPPC4 papers concern cancer, eQTL or unrelated contexts and do not affect the conclusion.

justification: Direct human genetic evidence with ASD phenotypes is reported in several independent primary studies: PMID 31300657 described heterozygous de novo GRIA2 variants in 28 unrelated patients with intellectual disability and neurodevelopmental abnormalities explicitly including autism spectrum disorder, with supporting functional electrophysiology; PMID 36329391 reported a de novo GRIA2 missense variant (p.Ala770Thr) in a patient with atypical ASD and psychiatric symptoms; PMID 35534222 reported a de novo p.Lys530Met variant in a child with ASD, global developmental delay and epileptic encephalopathy; and PMID 38572415 identified a de novo GRIA2 variant in an ASD proband in a Middle Eastern cohort. These are independent probands from different groups, with single-gene (not multigene CNV) variants, satisfying replication. Additional reports (PMID 34899870, 36161652, 38224558) describe the GRIA2-related neurodevelopmental disorder spectrum with autistic features, and an ASD patient-derived iPSC line carrying a GRIA2 mutation (PMID 35134694) adds model support. A small residual probability for "Existing" remains because ASD is typically one component of a broader GRIA2 neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than an isolated autism diagnosis.

justification: No article in this set reports LRRTM2 variants in ASD probands or families. The only human genetic study focused on LRRTM2 (PMID 23326251) concerns multigene 5q31 microdeletions and intellectual disability/developmental delay, and its own sequencing of 330 ID/DD patients found no relevant LRRTM2 alterations — i.e., negative human evidence, and a multigene deletion cannot implicate LRRTM2 specifically. The ASD-related human genetic findings here involve NRXN1/NRXN2/NRXN3 variants (PMIDs 21424692, 31578233, 39231636, 34168285), where LRRTM2 serves only as an in vitro binding partner used to assay the mutant neurexins. Remaining support is biological/mechanistic: LRRTM2 is a postsynaptic neurexin ligand driving excitatory synapse formation and AMPA receptor stabilization, with mouse knockout and synaptogenesis assays linking it to pathways repeatedly implicated in autism (PMIDs 20519524, 29784826, 30100184, 30262834, 38450720). This supports a plausible, biologically grounded but genetically unproven relationship, i.e., Hypothesized.
